issues.legal_issue: A procedural revenue-courts enactment did not repeal an existing substantive right to seek summary recovery of rent, although it changed the forum and removed the limitation bar for the application.
material_facts: An existing tenancy law gave a landlord a substantive right, following a government notification, to recover rent as arrears of land revenue.
A later enactment concerned the jurisdiction and procedure of revenue courts and officers, rather than creating or regulating the substantive right to recover rent.
The later enactment’s schedule listed applications for recovery of rent as land revenue, assigned them to a Collector, and prescribed no limitation period.
issues.conclusion: The substantive right continued. The application was to be made to a Collector, rather than a Deputy Commissioner, and was not subject to a limitation period under the later enactment.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2 of the Rajasthan Revenue Courts (Procedure and Jurisdiction) Act, 1951, an existing law was repealed only insofar as it related to matters dealt with by that Act. Section 85 of the Marwar Tenancy Act, 1949, created a substantive right that the later Act did not itself regulate. The schedule to the later Act recognised the relevant application and, read with sections 7 and 9, assigned it to a Collector without a limitation period. The provisions of the Tenancy Act concerning revenue-court jurisdiction and procedure, including sections 118, 124 and 129 and the corresponding schedule entry, were displaced to that extent, but section 85 remained in force.

predicates.application_for_summary_rent_recovery: The proceeding sought summary recovery of rent as land revenue under an existing tenancy law.
predicates.later_enactment_is_procedural_only: The later enactment dealt with the jurisdiction and procedure of revenue courts and officers, not the substantive right to recover rent.
predicates.earlier_law_creates_substantive_recovery: The earlier law gave a landlord a substantive right to seek recovery of rent as land revenue after a government notification.
predicates.later_schedule_recognizes_application_an: The later enactment’s schedule listed this kind of application, assigned it to a revenue officer, and prescribed no limitation period.

issues.definition: When an application seeks summary rent recovery under an earlier law that creates a substantive right, a later enactment limited to revenue-court jurisdiction and procedure does not remove that right when its schedule recognises the application and specifies its forum and limitation treatment.

issues.legal_issue: A summary application to recover rent as land revenue did not require notice to or a hearing for the tenant, and the contested-proceeding procedure did not apply.
material_facts: The government had issued a notification declaring that there was a general refusal to pay rent in the relevant area.
A landlord applied under the summary recovery procedure, and the revenue authority determined the amount due without notifying or hearing the tenants.
The tenants sought to have the contested-proceeding rules applied, which would have required notice and a hearing.
The governing tenancy law provided a later suit for a tenant from whom more than the amount due had been recovered.
issues.conclusion: The application was properly heard and determined without notice to the tenants. Applying the contested-proceeding rules would have defeated the summary procedure’s purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Section 85 of the Marwar Tenancy Act, 1949, contemplated an ex parte proceeding: it did not require notice, the notification had already declared a general refusal to pay, recovery as land revenue was summary, and section 85(4)(b) contemplated a later suit to challenge an excess recovery. Rule 114 and Chapter II of the rules under the Rajasthan Revenue Courts (Procedure and Jurisdiction) Act, 1951, did not displace that procedure; the right and its integral procedure continued together. The procedure under sections 78 and 80 of the Tenancy Act was contested and distinct from this summary remedy.

rule.if: application_for_summary_rent_recovery and notification_declared_general_refusal and recovery_used_summary_revenue_process and tenant_had_later_remedy_for_excess

predicates.application_for_summary_rent_recovery: A landlord applied for summary recovery of rent as land revenue.
predicates.notification_declared_general_refusal: The government issued a notification declaring a general refusal to pay rent in the relevant area.
predicates.recovery_used_summary_revenue_process: The proceeding sought recovery through the summary process used to collect land revenue.
predicates.tenant_had_later_remedy_for_excess: The governing law allowed a tenant to bring a later suit if more than the amount due had been recovered.

issues.definition: When a summary rent-recovery application follows a notification declaring a general refusal, uses the summary revenue-collection process, and leaves a later remedy for excess recovery, notice and a hearing for the tenant are not required.

issues.legal_issue: Rescission of a notification after a properly made rent-recovery application did not remove the revenue authority’s power to decide that pending application.
material_facts: A government notification covered the relevant area and permitted rent to be recovered as land revenue.
The landlord filed a proper application while the notification was in force.
The government rescinded the notification while the application was still pending.
The revenue authority had not yet completed the proceeding when the rescission occurred.
issues.conclusion: The rescission did not divest the revenue authority of power to dispose of the application, and recovery steps could continue on an amount found due.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 85(2) of the Marwar Tenancy Act, 1949, the words referring to a local area to which a notification applied concerned the area, not the period during which the notification remained in force. Once a proper application was made while the notification applied, the authority’s power to decide it was vested and was not removed by later rescission. The limitation entry in the Tenancy Act’s schedule, and its later displacement by the Rajasthan Revenue Courts (Procedure and Jurisdiction) Act, 1951, supported that reading. Crown v. Haveli, A.I.R. 1949 Lah. 191, concerning the expiry of a temporary Act, was distinguished because a provision activated by notification was not for that reason a temporary enactment.

predicates.application_for_summary_rent_recovery: The proceeding was an application for summary recovery of rent as land revenue.
predicates.notification_applied_to_area: A government notification permitting that recovery covered the area in which the rent was due.
predicates.application_properly_filed_while_notific: The landlord filed a proper application while the notification applied to the area.
predicates.notification_later_rescinded_before_deci: The government rescinded the notification after the application was filed but before the authority decided it.

issues.definition: When a proper summary rent-recovery application is filed while a notification applies to the area, later rescission before the decision does not remove the authority’s power to decide the pending application.

issues.legal_issue: A new challenge to the validity of a notification, not raised in the courts below and requiring factual and interpretive determinations, need not be considered for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The tenants argued before the Supreme Court that most tenants had paid rent and the remaining tenants were willing to pay but disputed the amount demanded.
The contention had not been raised in the High Court.
Deciding the contention would have required determining disputed facts about tenants’ conduct and interpreting the meaning of a general refusal to pay.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to allow the tenants to raise the contention for the first time on appeal and did not decide the notification’s validity on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a contention first raised on appeal where it depended on unresolved factual questions and an interpretation that had not been argued or considered at an earlier stage. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court: The matter was an appeal to the Supreme Court.
predicates.contention_not_raised_in_courts_below: The party had not raised the contention before the courts below.
predicates.contention_requires_unresolved_facts_and: Deciding the contention required resolving factual matters and interpreting a disputed legal expression.

issues.definition: In an appeal, a contention not raised below may be declined when its decision requires resolving facts and interpretation that were not previously considered.
